title: Push rejected: a 300MB file buried five commits back
intro: Your push is rejected: 'remote: error: File data/export.sql is 312.00 MB; this exceeds GitHub's file size limit of 100.00 MB'. You already deleted the file and committed that, but the push still fails. Five commits on your branch are unpushed.

steps.prompt: Find the biggest objects in your repository's history: list all objects with their sizes, sort by size, and show the top 3.
expected_commands: git rev-list --objects --all | git cat-file --batch-check='%(objecttype) %(objectname) %(objectsize) %(rest)' | sort -k3 -n -r | head -3
git rev-list --objects --all | git cat-file --batch-check='%(objecttype) %(objectname) %(objectsize) %(rest)' | sort -k3nr | head -3

blob 2d1c0b9a8f7e6d5c4b3a29181716151413121110 912384 package-lock.json

steps.prompt: Stop it happening again: ignore the data directory's SQL dumps by appending 'data/*.sql' to .gitignore.
steps.fake_output: (no output: the rule was appended to .gitignore)

resolution: Git stores every version of every file, so a file that was added and then deleted is still in history, and a push sends the whole history. That's why deleting it in a new commit didn't help: the commit that added it still had to be uploaded. Because the commits were unpushed, rewriting them was safe and affected nobody. (filter-repo removes the 'origin' remote as a safety measure on existing clones; add it back before pushing.) Had the file already been pushed and pulled by others, the rewrite would need a coordinated force-push and everyone re-cloning. For files that really do belong with the code, such as design assets or test fixtures, use Git LFS, which keeps a small pointer in Git and the content elsewhere. Database dumps don't belong in Git at all: store them in object storage and fetch them with a script.
